tier_reason: The README's 'Results on AMD zen4' section gives first-party numbers on a Ryzen 9 7950X3D: LeMac oneshot at 76.7 GiB/s (256 kB) and 74.3 GiB/s (1 MB), against SHA1 at about 2.8 GiB/s from `openssl speed -evp SHA1` on the same machine. The benchmark code is public (benchmark/benchmark.cpp) and flags can be read from CMakeLists.txt, but the compiler is not named for the Zen4 run and the baselines were measured with outside tools (openssl speed, xxhsum -b, clhash's own benchmark), so this stays at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: LeMac oneshot 76.7 GiB/s (256 kB) and 74.3 GiB/s (1 MB), median of 5 runs, vs about 2.8 GiB/s for OpenSSL SHA1 (`openssl speed -evp SHA1`) on the same AMD Ryzen 9 7950X3D, i.e. ~26-27x (derived from page data). The same README also reports: xxh3/xxh128 reach about 89 GiB/s with `xxhsum -b`, 'about 16% faster than lemac' (LeMac does not beat xxh3); clhash reaches 0.11 cycles/byte vs LeMac's 0.067 cycles/byte, which the README states as clhash being 'about 39% slower than lemac' (equivalently LeMac ~1.6x clhash throughput, derived from page data); raw AES-128-ECB (`openssl speed -evp AES-128-ECB`) reaches about 16.4 GiB/s. On a Raspberry Pi 5, LeMac does about 11.4 GiB/s against 13.2 GiB/s for xxh and 3.4 GiB/s for AES-128-ECB.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, with per-file flags from CMakeLists.txt on gcc/clang: -maes -msse2 for the AES-NI-128 path, and -maes -mvaes -mavx512f -mavx512vl for the VAES/AVX-512 path. The compiler is not named for the Zen4/Linux run (the README says Linux support is clang>=16 and gcc>=12); 'compiler: clang' is printed only for the Apple M3/M4 runs.
corrections.caveats: The README compares only against SHA1 (OpenSSL EVP), raw AES-128-ECB (OpenSSL), xxh3/xxh128 (xxhsum -b) and clhash. It has no comparison against a MAC incumbent such as GMAC/GHASH, Poly1305, HMAC or AEGIS. LeMac is a nonce-based MAC, so beating SHA1 (a bare digest) is not a like-for-like comparison and is best read as directional evidence of AES-NI-class speed. LeMac loses to xxh3 on Zen4 and to xxh on the Pi 5. The compiler is not named for the primary Zen4 run, and the baseline numbers come from outside tools rather than the repo's benchmark. This port implements the corrected LeMac from the ToSC 2025(1) corrigendum (DOI 10.46586/tosc.v2025.i1.623-628), not LeMac-0. src/lemac_aesni_impl.h and src/lemac_arm64_v8A.cpp use the extra RR message-schedule register and 'Four final rounds', as in upstream commit d035564f 'Fix LeMac specification, and rename erroneous version as LeMac-0' (Oct 2024). test/tests.cpp asserts the corrected 'LeMac' test vectors (for example 52282e853c9cfeb5537d33fb916a341f for the empty message) rather than the LeMac-0 ones. Arm64 on Windows has no runtime check for hardware support.

notes: LeMac is the corrected version from the corrigendum, not LeMac-0. The code matches upstream's fix (RR register, four final zero rounds) and the tests check the upstream 'LeMac' (v1) vectors. The corrigendum fixed a mismatch between the published message schedule and the MILP-analysed design (25 vs 26 active S-boxes), not a padding bug. The README compares against SHA1, AES-128-ECB, xxh3/xxh128 and clhash, never against a MAC incumbent. It wins against SHA1 (~27x), AES-ECB and clhash, and loses to xxh3 by about 16%. The only wording fix is the clhash comparison.

tier_reason: rurban/smhasher is a well-known independent suite. Its main table on the stated CPU (AMD Ryzen 5 3350G 3.6GHz) lists SpookyV2_64 at 13401.13 MiB/s, 56.18 cycles/hash and 246.33 cycles/map, against xxHash64 at 11176.72 MiB/s, 49.67 cycles/hash and 230.24 cycles/map. The code is public, but neither the README nor doc/SpookyV2_64.txt names the compiler or flags, so this is B, not A.

corrections.workload: rurban/smhasher main table on an AMD Ryzen 5 3350G. MiB/sec is the average bulk speed over alignments 0-7 with 262144-byte keys. cycl./hash is the average of the small-key speed test over 1-31 byte keys. cycl./map is a C++ hashmap get test over /usr/dict/words. Rows compared: SpookyV2_32/64/128 vs xxHash64, xxh3 and City64 on the same machine.
corrections.caveats: rurban/smhasher states the CPU (AMD Ryzen 5 3350G) for its main table but not the compiler or flags, so this is capped at tier B. SpookyV2 beats xxHash64 only on large-buffer bulk throughput. On small keys (cycles/hash, averaged over 1-31 byte keys) and in the hashmap test (cycles/map) it is slower than xxHash64, and xxh3 and City64 beat it in every column. The GitHub repo was created on 2026-03-28, but its history starts on 2025-12-23. It is Bob Jenkins' own repo: burtleburtle.net/bob/hash/spooky.html links to it and the commits are by Robert J Jenkins Jr. Its cplus/SpookyV2.cpp and cplus/SpookyV2.h are identical, apart from CRLF line endings, to the SpookyV2.cpp/.h that rurban/smhasher builds for its SpookyV2_32/64/128 rows, so those rows measure exactly this repo's C++ code. SpookyHash V1 (the 'UB' Spooky32/64/128 rows) was removed from this repo in Feb 2026. The repo also has a new Rust port, which Claude generated according to the README. The README's own throughput table (DoTimingSmall, g++ -O3, one unnamed machine) compares only C++ with Rust and includes no baseline hash. The Unlicense is a public-domain dedication with no patent grant.

notes: bobjen/spookyhash contains the reference SpookyV2 code that the rurban/smhasher SpookyV2 rows measure. cplus/SpookyV2.cpp and .h diff clean against rurban's copies once CRLF endings are ignored, and burtleburtle.net links to this repo as the official source. That makes it a sound replacement for the archived g1mv/spookyhash C port. All numbers match rurban's README. They come from rurban/smhasher, not SMHasher3, which I did not check.
